tier_reason: The README 'Performance evidence' table gives per-family speedups over legacy Clipper2, with compiler and flags (GCC 13.1 -O3 -DNDEBUG; MSVC 19.44 /O2 /Ob2 /DNDEBUG) and Google Benchmark settings. The benchmark code is public in benchmarks/ (oracle/, product/, tools/; presets linux-gcc-oracle-benchmarks and msvc-oracle-benchmarks). No CPU model is stated anywhere I opened, only 'the Linux release runner', and the raw JSON is kept out of Git. That makes it first-party with partial methodology, so C.

corrections.claimed_speedup: Release-gate results for version 5.0.1 against legacy Clipper2 (README). Linux (GCC 13.1, -O3): 14-pair geometric mean 1.615x; intersection 1.584x, union 1.669x, difference 1.694x, XOR 1.715x, offset 1.770x, triangulation 2.340x, Minkowski 1.454x, unprepared RectClip 1.247x (lowest). Windows (MSVC 19.44 /O2): geometric mean 1.758x, labelled directional because other benchmarks exceeded the 5% CV ceiling (intersection 1.487x, offset 1.563x, triangulation 2.878x, open-line RectClip 4.287x). The README says versions 6.1.x make no new performance claim.
corrections.is_fork_of: https://github.com/AngusJohnson/Clipper2 (NOTICE.md: 'historically derived from Clipper2 by Angus Johnson', BSL-1.0, being refactored into new modules; not a GitHub fork)
corrections.caveats: No CPU model is stated, so this falls short of tier A, and the raw benchmark JSON is not in Git. All numbers are the author's own, from the 5.0.1 release gate, against the author's build of 'legacy' Clipper2. The speedups are for the default/unprepared APIs, and the 6.x releases make no new speed claim. The author flags the Windows result as noisy. The code is derived from Clipper2 (per NOTICE.md), so this is a modernized fork that is faster than its parent. It requires C++23 (std::expected), which limits where it can be used. The repo is about four weeks old (first commit 2026-09-03, 8 commits) with one star. There is no comparison against Boost.Geometry, GEOS or CGAL.

notes: All Linux and Windows ratios in the record match the README table. I added the provenance from NOTICE.md (derived from Clipper2; Clipper2 itself is not in the catalog, so this is not a duplicate) and the 5.0.1/6.x context. BSL-1.0, 1 star, last commit 2026-09-30 and not a GitHub fork all confirmed.

tier_reason: The README has a box-plot chart (doc/images/coal-vs-the-rest-of-the-world.png) of per-query GJK times for Coal against libccd, FCL and Bullet, plus a '5x up to 15x' sentence. It states no hardware, compiler, flags or harness. The RSS 2022 artifact repo (lmontaut/collision-detection-benchmark) compares only vanilla and Nesterov GJK inside HPP-FCL, not FCL, libccd or Bullet. The chart probably comes from the authors' peer-reviewed GJK++ paper (IEEE T-RO 2024), but I could not open it to confirm, so it stays C.

corrections.claimed_speedup: README: the accelerated GJK variants 'largely outperform by a large margin (from 5x up to 15x times faster)'. Medians read from the README box plot (log scale, approximate, derived from page data): Nesterov about 1.1 us, Polyak about 1.2 us, Coal vanilla GJK about 1.6 us; libccd MPR and GJK about 4.2 us; FCL GJK about 9.5 us; Bullet GJK about 17 us. That puts Nesterov at about 3.8x over libccd, 8.6x over FCL and 15x over Bullet, and vanilla Coal GJK at about 6x over FCL (derived from page data). Against libccd the medians do not reach the README's lower bound of 5x.
corrections.is_fork_of: https://github.com/flexible-collision-library/fcl (hard fork in 2015 as HPP-FCL, renamed Coal in 2024, per the README; not a GitHub fork)
corrections.stars_or_usage: 645 stars, 157 forks; README lists Pinocchio, IfcOpenShell, Crocoddyl, TSID, HPP, Jiminy, ocs2 and Simple as users; on conda-forge and PyPI
corrections.caveats: The evidence is one README chart, labelled with the pre-2024 'HPP-FCL' name. It states no hardware, compiler, flags, shapes or harness, and no benchmark code for the cross-library comparison is linked. The RSS 2022 artifact repo lmontaut/collision-detection-benchmark (g++ 9.4/12.1 and clang++ 13.0.1, no CPU or flags) covers only vanilla vs Nesterov GJK inside HPP-FCL. The cross-library figure is probably from the GJK++ paper (IEEE T-RO 2024, hal-04070039), which I could not open. The README's '5x' lower bound overstates the gap to libccd (about 3.8x at the median). The baseline FCL is Coal's own ancestor, and none of the category's list (Boost.Geometry, CGAL, GEOS, R-tree) is compared. Narrow-phase collision detection is only loosely 'geometry-spatial'.

notes: The chart medians in the record match my own reading of the image. The README's 5x-15x is accurate only against FCL and Bullet; against libccd it is about 3.8x. I could not reach the GJK++ T-RO paper (hal.science, arxiv.org and simple-robotics.github.io are egress-blocked); if a later check confirms it contains this figure with stated hardware, the entry could move to B. BSD-3-Clause (LICENSE text), last commit 2026-09-30 and not a GitHub fork confirmed.

tier_reason: The QuickHull.h doc comment and the module documentation source (src/DGtal/geometry/doc/moduleQuickHull.dox) both say only 'generally more than twice faster than CGAL convex_hull_3' for the Cartesian and EPICK kernels. Neither gives CGAL timings, point counts or a benchmark program. This first-party ratio claim without methodology sits at the C/D border; it is kept at C because a >2x figure is stated.

corrections.claimed_speedup: Source doc comment and module docs: 'This version is generally more than twice faster than CGAL convex_hull_3 for the usual CGAL kernels Cartesian and Exact_predicates_inexact_constructions_kernel.' No CGAL timings are given. The same docs say that Delaunay triangulation via the higher-dimensional convex hull is 'generally much slower than CGAL method ... (5-10 times slower in our experience)'. DGtal-only timings (MacBook Pro, 2.7 GHz quad-core Intel Core i7): 1e7 random lattice points in a ball of radius 1000 take 7913 ms in total, of which 4221 ms purge duplicates and 3214 ms is the QuickHull core.
corrections.caveats: The claim is a single qualitative sentence, repeated in the module docs, with no CGAL numbers, point distributions, flags or compiler. The only timings are DGtal's own, on a MacBook Pro i7 2.7 GHz quad-core. Only the 3D convex hull is claimed faster. The docs themselves say the Delaunay use is 5-10x slower than CGAL's Delaunay triangulation. Unlike CGAL, the hull is not simplicial (facets may be polygons). The exact lattice kernels are about 25x slower when BigInteger is used for the internal integers. The QuickHull module is part of the much larger LGPL DGtal library.

notes: The claim is verbatim in QuickHull.h (lines 131-133) and in moduleQuickHull.dox, which I read from the source tree instead of the unreachable rendered docs page. I added the docs' own counter-statement that Delaunay is 5-10x slower than CGAL, and the DGtal-only timings. LGPL-3.0-or-later (file header), 398 stars, last commit 2026-09-23 and not a fork confirmed.
